summary: MPLS-TP supports point-to-point and point-to-multipoint transport paths. This document defines the elements and functions of MPLS-TP for point-to-multipoint paths, as a framework.

eli5.summary: One sender needs to reach many receivers over a carrier network. This describes the parts and rules needed.

subtitle: How MPLS Transport Profile sends data from one source to multiple destinations.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is designed as a carrier-grade transport technology for packet networks, but initially focused on point-to-point paths. Carriers need point-to-multipoint paths to support services like video distribution and IP multicast, analogous to traditional transport technologies.
tldr.mechanism: This framework document describes the MPLS-TP architecture for point-to-multipoint (P2MP) transport paths, including unidirectional LSPs and PWs, operations and maintenance functions, control plane protocols, recovery mechanisms, and network management.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7167 provides a roadmap for implementing and operating P2MP services in MPLS-TP networks, referencing existing MPLS specifications and identifying areas needing further development, especially for P2MP pseudowires.

today: RFC 7167 is an Informational document published in April 2014. It remains the authoritative framework for MPLS-TP point-to-multipoint services. P2MP LSPs have seen successful deployment in service provider networks for video distribution and IP multicast services. The follow-up work on formal recovery definitions and P2MP PW specifications has continued in IETF working groups, though adoption of P2MP PWs has been slower than P2MP LSPs. The framework is stable and widely referenced in MPLS-TP deployments.

sections.title: Point-to-Multipoint in Transport Networks
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a subset of MPLS designed specifically for carrier transport networks. It offers the operational rigor, fault detection, and management capabilities that service providers demand. MPLS-TP initially focused on point-to-point paths where one source connects to one destination. However, carriers need point-to-multipoint (P2MP) paths to deliver services like video distribution, IPTV, and IP multicast to many customers from a single source.

This document extends the MPLS-TP framework (defined in RFC 5921) to cover P2MP transport paths. Traditional transport technologies such as Optical Transport Network (OTN) have long supported P2MP through drop-and-continue mechanisms: a signal flows down a link, and intermediate nodes can extract and forward a copy to downstream branches. MPLS-TP P2MP operates on the same principle but at the packet/label level.
sections.eli5: One sender (like a video studio) connects to one path down a tree-shaped network. At each branch point, a copy goes down each path. Every destination gets the same video.

sections.title: What P2MP Must Support
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes requirements from RFC 5654, RFC 5860, and RFC 5951. MPLS-TP must support unidirectional P2MP transport paths: a single sender reaches multiple receivers, without a reverse path. P2MP paths must be traffic engineered, meaning the operator can specify the exact path the traffic takes, ensuring quality of service guarantees. The control plane must support establishing P2MP connectivity and configuring protection (recovery from failures).

Operations and maintenance (OAM) functions critical for transport networks must work with P2MP paths: continuity checks (is the path working?), connectivity verification (is traffic reaching all leaves?), packet loss measurement, packet delay measurement, and alarm reporting. Recovery must work: if a link fails, traffic should switch to a backup path with minimal disruption. Unidirectional 1+1 and 1:n protection must be supported, where backup paths carry redundant copies or stand ready to take over.
sections.eli5: The operator picks the exact paths. All leaves must get the traffic. If a pipe breaks, automatic backup takes over. The network must monitor health and report problems.

sections.title: MPLS-TP P2MP Architecture
sections.content:
The P2MP architecture comprises two main transport entity types:

P2MP Label Switched Paths (LSPs) are the primary mechanism. A Label Switched Path (LSP) is a path through MPLS routers (Label Switching Routers, or LSRs) where each hop forwards traffic based on a label (a short identifier) rather than a long IP address. A P2MP LSP has a root LSR (the sender) and one or more leaf LSRs (receivers). Each LSP is unidirectional: traffic flows from the root toward all leaves, but not back. The encapsulation and forwarding of P2MP LSPs is identical to MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) P2MP LSPs, defined in RFC 4875.

P2MP Pseudowires (PWs) are a second, emerging mechanism. Pseudowires emulate services (like Ethernet virtual circuits) over MPLS. P2MP PW specifications are still under development and marked for further study; the RFC notes that encapsulation and forwarding for P2MP PWs have not yet been formally defined.

MPLS-TP P2MP supports both upstream-assigned and downstream-assigned labels: labels chosen by the sending router or by each downstream router along the path.
sections.eli5: A P2MP LSP is like a river that branches at each fork, sending water (traffic) down every branch. Each branch is labeled so routers know where to send packets. PWs are a newer way to do it, still being designed.

sections.title: Operations, Maintenance, and Management
sections.content:
Operations and Maintenance (OAM) in P2MP paths presents unique challenges because all traffic—including OAM packets generated at the root—flows multicast toward all leaves. If an OAM packet must be processed by only one specific leaf, the sender must indicate this with a special tag. The RFC uses Time-to-Live (TTL)-based addressing to set the "radius" of an OAM packet (how many hops it travels), and additional payload information to identify the specific destination leaf.

P2MP paths are unidirectional, so any response to an OAM query must return via an out-of-band path (a separate channel, not part of the main P2MP path). This complicates fault detection: a leaf cannot directly report problems to the root; the network must use an alternate path.

Network management follows the framework in RFC 5951, which derives requirements from ITU-T standards for transport networks. P2MP paths require Management Information Base (MIB) modules for SNMP-based management. The RFC references ongoing work on P2MP-specific MIBs to manage configuration, performance, and faults.
sections.eli5: Checking if a path works is tricky: a message sent to all leaves must say "only leaf #3 needs to answer." Replies come back a different way. Management tools must track and report on all those branches.

sections.title: Control Plane and Recovery
sections.content:
The control plane is the mechanism for establishing and managing paths. For P2MP LSPs, MPLS-TP uses GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) and RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol with Traffic Engineering extensions). GMPLS is a generalization of MPLS that handles various types of data-plane devices; RFC 4875 defines RSVP-TE for P2MP LSPs. The control plane must communicate topology information, reserve bandwidth, signal which paths to use, and orchestrate recovery actions.

For P2MP Pseudowires, the control plane should use LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) with P2MP extensions. LDP is used for point-to-point PWs; extending it to P2MP is still under development and marked for further study.

Recovery and protection in P2MP is more complex than in point-to-point. 1+1 protection means the root sends traffic down both a working and a protection path; each leaf independently selects which copy to use. 1:n protection means multiple backup paths stand by; if the primary fails, traffic switches to a backup, and multiple failures can be protected. The RFC notes that recovery techniques for P2MP LSPs were not formally defined at the time and should be documented. More sophisticated approaches like partial tree protection and 1:n shared mesh recovery are identified as future work.
sections.eli5: The control plane tells every router: "send this customer's video down this tree of pipes using label 1234." If a pipe breaks, a backup tree takes over. For very complex networks, fancier backup strategies are being designed.

sections.title: Current Status and Future Work
sections.content:
RFC 7167 is a framework document that codifies the P2MP aspects of MPLS-TP. At the time of publication (April 2014), P2MP LSPs were well defined and could be deployed, building on prior work in MPLS Traffic Engineering. However, several areas were identified for further work: formal definition of recovery techniques for traffic-engineered P2MP LSPs, the complete control plane specification for P2MP pseudowires, encapsulation and forwarding definitions for P2MP PWs, and more sophisticated survivability approaches.

The RFC emphasizes that P2MP PWs are marked "for further study" because at that time, there was insufficient operational experience to define them fully. Over subsequent years, standards development continued on P2MP services, though P2MP PWs remain less widely deployed than P2MP LSPs.
sections.eli5: P2MP LSPs (the main tree-path mechanism) were ready to use. P2MP PWs (simulating circuits) were still being designed. Later work has made them better, but trees are more common than circuit simulations.
